111.0501pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut$}}}}$}}

Here the left side of the rewriting rule is associated to the bl-graph

\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis\odot_{(A\lor(B\land C))}(\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis\sqcup\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis),

while the right side is interpreted as

(\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis\odot_{A}\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis)\odot_{B\land C}\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis;

the conjunction
B\land C
is contained in the interface in the former expression, where
the interpretation is computed by a single composition step, but lies outside the interface
in the first half of the latter expression, where we compute first the intermediate step

\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis\odot_{A}\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis
. To show that this is an actual problem, not just a hypothetical
possibility, we provide a complete (but slightly involved) counter-example in
fig.

6
.

It remains unclear whether there is some syntactical counterpart to the semantical cut-elimination
procedure described in
section

6.2
. It is possible that the problem could be
solved simply by superposing the two reducts, thus making the rewriting step deterministic:

\cdot

P

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A,B\vphantom{\overline{A}}\mathstrut

\cdot

\mathtt{wk}(Q,B)

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{A},B\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,B\mathstrut

\cdot

R

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{B}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

\cdot

P

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A,B\vphantom{\overline{B}}\mathstrut

\cdot

\mathtt{wk}(R,A)

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A,\overline{B}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A\mathstrut

\cdot

Q

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{A}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

\mathtt{\sqcup}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

We have not been able to find a counter-example so far, but we have yet to attempt a proof.
We would have to show somehow that whenever some path is erased on one side, then it
must be preserved on the other side, and
vice versa
.

A different possibility would be to further refine the interpretation so as to make it
invariant under the two traditional cut-reduction steps. The key observation in this regard
is that all counter-examples known to us – including indeed the one in
fig.

6

– seem to rely critically on the possibility of constructing alternating paths using edges
from both branches of a superposition rule. This happens because superposition is not
interpreted as a non-deterministic sum of separate proofs, but as some kind of parallel
composition that “blends” two proofs together, thus obtaining a new and generally distinct one.
We conjecture that by treating superpositions as proper non-deterministic sums we should be
able to recover invariance under the traditional logical reduction steps. The picture however
is complicated by the fact that superpositions might be introduced when reducing weakening-weakening cuts: it is not clear then how the new composition operator should look like.

Appendix 0.A
Graphs

Definition 20

(Simple graphs)
.

A
graph
(also known as
simple graph
) is defined by a pair

G=\langle V_{G},E_{G}\rangle
where
V_{G}
is a set of
vertices
and

E_{G}
is a set of unordered pairs of vertices, i.e.
two-element subsets

of
V_{G}
, called the
edges of
G
. For any pair of distinct vertices

u\neq v\in V_{G}
, let
uv
denote the set
\{u,v\}
and say that
u

and
v
are
adjacent
in
G
iff
uv\in E_{G}
.

Definition 21

(Subgraphs)
.

Given graphs
H,G
, say that
H
is a subgraph of
G
and write

H\sqsubseteq G
iff
V_{H}\subseteq V_{G}
and
E_{H}\subseteq E_{G}
. Write

H\sqsubset G
iff
H\sqsubseteq G
and
H\neq G
.

Given a graph
G
, any set
S
of vertices induces a subgraph
H\sqsubseteq G

by letting
V_{H}=V_{H}\cap S
and restricting the edge set:

E_{H}=\{e\in E_{G}\mid e\subseteq S\}.

We say that
H
is an
induced subgraph
of
G
and denote it by
G{\upharpoonright}_{S}
.

Graphs can be combined by an operation related to set-theoretic union, which constructs the least
upper bound of a family of graphs w.r.t. the subgraph order
{\sqsubseteq}
:

Definition 22

(Graph union)
.

Let
I
be a set,
(G_{i})_{i\in I}
a family of graphs indexed by
I
. We define
the
union
or
superposition
of the family as the graph

\bigsqcup_{i\in I}G_{i}=\langle\bigcup_{i\in I}V_{G_{i}},\bigcup_{i\in I}E_{G_{i}}\rangle.

As a special case, given
n\geq 0
and graphs
G_{1},\ldots,G_{n}
, we define the
finite union

G_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup G_{n}=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}.

Proposition 6

Let
I
be a set,
(G_{i})_{i\in I}
a family of graphs indexed by
I
; the union
graph
\bigsqcup_{i\in I}G_{i}
is the least upper bound of the family w.r.t. the
subgraph order
{\sqsubseteq}
.

Proposition 7

Let
I
be any set,
(G_{i})_{i\in I}
a family of graphs indexed by
I
,
S
an
arbitrary set of vertices: then

\left(\bigsqcup_{i\in I}G_{i}\right){\upharpoonright}_{S}=\bigsqcup_{i\in I}(G_{i}{\upharpoonright}_{S})

Appendix 0.B
Complexity measures on formulas, sequents and derivations

We define in the following paragraphs some useful measures of the complexity of formulas,
sequents and derivations, and discuss the relationships between them.

Definition 23

(Complexity of formulas)
.

We define by structural induction four different measures on named formulas
A
:
the
height

\mathtt{h}(A)
, the
atom count

\mathtt{\#at}(A)
, the

degree

\mathtt{deg}(A)
and the
size

\mathtt{size}(A)
:

•

if
A
is atomic, let

\displaystyle\mathtt{h}(A)=\mathtt{deg}(A)=0,

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(A)=\mathtt{size}(A)=1;

•

if
A=B\lor C
or
A=B\land C
, let

\displaystyle\mathtt{h}(A)

\displaystyle=1+\max\{\mathtt{h}(B),\mathtt{h}(C)\},

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(A)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{\#at}(B)+\mathtt{\#at}(C),

\displaystyle\mathtt{deg}(A)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(B)+\mathtt{deg}(C),

\displaystyle\mathtt{size}(A)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{size}(B)+\mathtt{size}(C).

The height tracks the length of the longest branch in the syntax tree of the formula,
the atom count is self-explanatory, the degree is the number of logical operators occurring
in the formula, and the size is the number of symbols (atoms and operators).

Proposition 8

For all named formulas
A
:

1.

\mathtt{\#at}(A)=1+\mathtt{deg}(A)
;

2.

\mathtt{size}(A)=\mathtt{\#at}(A)+\mathtt{deg}(A)=1+2\cdot\mathtt{deg}(A)
;

3.

\mathtt{h}(A)\leq\mathtt{deg}(A)<\mathtt{\#at}(A)\leq\mathtt{size}(A)
.

Proof.

The inequalities
\deg(A)<\mathtt{\#at}(A)
and
\mathtt{\#at}(A)\leq\mathtt{size}(A)

are direct consequences of facts (i) and (ii). We prove facts (i) and (ii) and the first
inequality simultaneously by structural induction on
A
:

•

if
A
is atomic, then

\displaystyle 0=\mathtt{h}(A)\leq\mathtt{deg}(A)=0,

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(A)=1=1+0=1+\mathtt{deg}(A)\text{, and}

\displaystyle\mathtt{size}(A)=1=1+0=\mathtt{\#at}(A)+\mathtt{deg}(A);

•

if
A=B\lor C
or
A=B\land C
, then

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(A)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{\#at}(B)+\mathtt{\#at}(C)

(def.
23
)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{deg}(B)+1+\mathtt{deg}(C)+1

(ind. hyp.)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(B)+\mathtt{deg}(C)+1

\displaystyle=\mathtt{deg}(A)+1

(def.
23
)

\displaystyle\mathtt{size}(A)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{size}(B)+\mathtt{size}(C)

(def.
23
)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{\#at}(B)+\mathtt{deg}(B)+\mathtt{\#at}(C)+\mathtt{deg}(C)

(ind. hyp.)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{\#at}(B)+\mathtt{\#at}(C)+1+\mathtt{deg}(B)+\mathtt{deg}(C)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{\#at}(A)+\mathtt{deg}(A)

(def.
23
)

\displaystyle\mathtt{h}(A)

\displaystyle=1+\max\{\mathtt{h}(B),\mathtt{h}(C)\}

(def.
23
)

\displaystyle\leq 1+\mathtt{h}(B)+\mathtt{h}(C)

\displaystyle\leq 1+\mathtt{deg}(B)+\mathtt{deg}(C)

(ind. hyp.)

\displaystyle=\mathtt{deg}(A)

(def.
23
)

∎

Definition 24

(Complexity of sequents)
.

We define for sequents the same measures as for formulas, by taking sums over all
formulas contained in the sequent: for all named sequents
\thesis\Gamma
let

\displaystyle\mathtt{h}(\thesis\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{h}(A),

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{\#at}(A),

\displaystyle\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{deg}(A),

\displaystyle\mathtt{size}(\thesis\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{size}(A).

Since
\Gamma
is required to be finite, all measures are well-defined.

Proposition 9

For all named sequents
\thesis\Gamma
:

1.

\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)=|\Gamma|+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Gamma)
;

2.

\mathtt{size}(\thesis\Gamma)=\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Gamma)=|\Gamma|+2\cdot\mathtt{deg}(A)
;

3.

\mathtt{h}(\thesis\Gamma)\leq\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Gamma)<\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)\leq\mathtt{size}(\thesis\Gamma)
.

Proof.

For fact (i), observe that

\displaystyle\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{\#at}(A)

(def.
24
)

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in\Gamma}1+\mathtt{deg}(A)

(lemma
8
(i))

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{A\in\Gamma}1\right)+\left(\sum_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{deg}(A)\right)

(associativity)

\displaystyle=\#\Gamma+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Gamma)

(def.
24
).

Fact (ii) follows from
definition

24
and the associativity of sums;
fact (iii) follows from
proposition

8
, point (iii) and
the fact that addition is strictly monotonic over the natural numbers.
∎

Definition 25

(Complexity of derivations)
.

We define by structural induction two complexity measures on named derivation
trees
P\in\mathtt{GS4}^{\mathcal{N}}
: the
height

\mathtt{h}(P)
and the

size

\mathtt{size}(P)
:

•

if
P
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A,\overline{B}\mathstrut

where
A\equiv B
, then let

\mathtt{h}(P)=0,\ \mathtt{size}(P)=1;

•

otherwise
P
has the form

\cdot

Q_{1}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma_{1}\mathstrut

\displaystyle\cdots\mathstrut

\cdot

Q_{n}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma_{n}\mathstrut

r

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

where
r\in\{\mathtt{cut},\mathtt{\sqcup},\mathtt{\lor},\mathtt{\land}\}

and
n>0
: then let

\displaystyle\mathtt{h}(P)

\displaystyle=1+\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\mathtt{h}(Q_{i}),

\displaystyle\mathtt{size}(P)

\displaystyle=1+\sum_{1\leq i\leq n}\mathtt{size}(Q_{i}).

be

\hbox{$\vbox{\vbox{\hbox{\enskip\hbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle{\hbox{$\vbox{\hbox{\hskip 26.24301pt\hbox{}}\hbox{\hskip 22.35413pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\raise 2.77779pt\hbox{\hbox{\raise 2.22221pt\hbox{\lower 2.22221pt\hbox{\hbox{\vbox to18.08325pt{\leaders{\hbox{$\cdot$}}{\vfill}}\hbox{\ }}}}}\thinspace\raise-0.27779pt\hbox{$\mathtt{wk}(\phi Q,\Delta)$}}}}\vbox{\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\phi A,\Delta\vphantom{\mkern 4.0mu\overline{\mkern-4.0mu(\phi A)\mkern-4.0mu}\mkern 4.0mu}\mathstrut$}}}}$}}\mathstrut$}\hbox{$\displaystyle\quad{\hbox{$\vbox{\hbox{\hskip 18.68051pt\hbox{}}\hbox{\hskip 14.79163pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\raise 2.77779pt\hbox{\hbox{\raise 2.22221pt\hbox{\lower 2.22221pt\hbox{\hbox{\vbox to18.08325pt{\leaders{\hbox{$\cdot$}}{\vfill}}\hbox{\ }}}}}\thinspace\raise-0.27779pt\hbox{$\mathtt{wk}(\phi R,\Delta)$}}}}\vbox{\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\mkern 4.0mu\overline{\mkern-4.0mu(\phi A)\mkern-4.0mu}\mkern 4.0mu,\Delta\mathstrut$}}}}$}}\mathstrut$}}}}\hbox{\hskip 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\raise 1.6915pt\hbox{\hbox{\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\raise 1.72218pt\hbox{\vrule width=134.4123pt,height=0.43057pt}}}\thinspace\raise-1.6915pt\hbox{$\mathtt{cut}$}}}}\vbox{\hbox{\hskip 54.6367pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\Delta\mathstrut$}}}}$}\qed

Appendix 0.D
Renamings

Definition 26
.

A
renaming
of a named formula
A
(resp. set
\Gamma
of named formulas) is an

injective map
from
\mathtt{names}(A)
(resp.
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
)
to
\mathcal{N}
. For any named formula
A
and renaming
\phi
of
A
, let

\phi A=\begin{cases}{\alpha}^{\phi x}&\text{if }A={\alpha}^{x}\text{ for some }\alpha\in\mathcal{A},x\in\mathcal{N},\\
\phi B\lor\phi C&\text{if }A=B\lor C,\\
\phi B\land\phi C&\text{if }A=B\land C.\end{cases}

The application of a renaming
\phi
to a set
\Gamma
is defined by taking its image
under
\phi
, observing that, for each
A\in\Gamma
, the restriction of
\phi

to
\mathtt{names}(A)
is necessarily a renaming of
A
.

Proposition 10

For any named formula
A
and renaming
\phi
of
A
,
\phi A
is also a named
formula with
A\equiv\phi A
,
\mathtt{names}(\phi A)=\phi(\mathtt{names}(A))
,
and sharing-free iff so is
A
.

Proof.

The equivalence result and that about name sets are more or less immediate, by structural
induction on
A
. As regards sharing-freedom, we reason again by structural induction
on
A
:

•

if
A
is atomic then so is
\phi A
and they are both sharing-free
by definition;

•

if
A=B\diamond C
(where
{\diamond}\in\{{\lor},{\land}\}
), then

\phi A=\phi B\diamond\phi C
. By induction hypothesis
B,C
are
sharing-free if and only if so are
\phi B,\phi C
, respectively. Moreover,
because
\phi
is injective,
\mathtt{names}(\phi B)=\phi(\mathtt{names}(B))

and the same holds for
C

mutatis mutandis
,
B,C
are disjoint
if and only if so are
\phi B,\phi C
. Then
A
is sharing-free, by definition,
iff
B,C
are disjoint and both sharing-free, iff
\phi B,\phi C
are disjoint
and both sharing-free, iff again by definition
\phi A
is sharing-free. ∎

Lemma 20

Let
A
be any named formula:

1.

\phi
is a renaming of
A
if and only if it is a renaming of
\overline{A}
;

2.

for any renaming
\phi
of
A
,
\phi(\overline{A})=\mkern 4.0mu\overline{\mkern-4.0mu(\phi A)\mkern-4.0mu}\mkern 4.0mu
.

Proof.

Left to the reader.
∎

Lemma 21

Let
\Gamma
be a set of named formulas,
\phi
a renaming of
\Gamma
:

1.

for all
A,B\in\Gamma
,
A=B
if and only if
\phi A=\phi B
;

2.

for all
A,B\in\Gamma
,
A,B
share names if and only if so do
\phi A,\phi B
;

3.

for all
\Delta,\Delta^{\prime}\subseteq\Gamma
,
\Delta,\Delta^{\prime}
share
names if and only if so do
\phi\Delta,\phi\Delta^{\prime}
.

Proof.

Point (ii) is a special case of point (iii), which is in turn an immediate consequence
of the injectivity of
\phi
plus the obvious facts that
\mathtt{names}(\phi\Delta)=\phi(\mathtt{names}(\Delta))
and
\mathtt{names}(\phi\Delta^{\prime})=\phi(\mathtt{names}(\Delta^{\prime}))
.
For point (i) we proceed by structural induction on
A
:

•

A
is atomic: then
A=B
if and only if
A={\alpha}^{x}=B

(resp.
A={\overline{\alpha}}^{x}=B
) for some
\alpha\in\mathcal{A}

and
x\in\mathcal{N}
, if and only if
\phi A={\alpha}^{\phi x}=\phi B

(resp.
\phi A={\overline{\alpha}}^{\phi x}=\phi B
);

•

A=C\diamond D
where
{\diamond}\in\{{\lor},{\land}\}
: then
A=B

if and only if
B=C\diamond D
, if and only if
\phi A=\phi C\lor\phi D=\phi B
. ∎

Corollary 7

For all named sequents
\thesis\Gamma
and renamings
\phi
of
\thesis\Gamma
,

\phi(\thesis\Gamma)
is also a named sequent with
(\thesis\Gamma)\equiv\phi(\thesis\Gamma)
,
and sharing-free iff so is
\thesis\Gamma
.

Proof.

The fact that
\phi(\thesis\Gamma)
is a named sequent and sharing-free iff so is
\thesis\Gamma
follows from
propositions

10
and
21
,
point (ii). For the equivalence, observe that by
lemma

21
, point (i),

\phi
induces a bijection between
\Gamma
and
\phi\Gamma
such that (again by

proposition

10
)
A\equiv\phi A
for all
A\in\Gamma
.
∎

Finally, we can rename whole derivation trees while preserving their structure and
conclusion (obviously up to renaming):

Definition 27
.

A
renaming
of a named derivation tree
P\in\mathtt{GS4}^{\mathcal{N}}
is an injective
map
\phi:\mathtt{names}(P)\to\mathcal{N}
.

The application of
\phi
to
P
, noted
\phi P
, is the tree obtained by applying
\phi

recursively to the named sequents labeling each node of
P
(plus the selected formulas in
axiom rules).

Proposition 11

Let
P\in\mathtt{GS4}^{\mathcal{N}}
be any named derivation tree with conclusion
\thesis\Gamma
,
\phi
a renaming of
P
: then
\phi P\in\mathtt{GS4}^{\mathcal{N}}

is also a derivation tree with conclusion
\phi(\thesis\Gamma)
and height
\mathtt{h}(\phi P)=\mathtt{h}(P)
, cut-free (resp. superposition-free) iff so is
P
.

Proof.

By a simple structural induction on
P
, using
proposition

10

and
corollary

7
to prove that constraints on the shape
of rules are satisfied by
\phi P
at every step.
∎

Appendix 0.E
Proofs of lemmas regarding simple axiom graphs

Proof of
proposition

1
.

By structural induction on
P
:

•

if
P
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A,\overline{B}\mathstrut

where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{A,\overline{B}\}
and
A\equiv B
then by

definitions

6
and
9

V_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=\mathtt{names}(\Delta)\cup\mathtt{names}(\{A,\overline{B}\})=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
;

•

if
P
has the form

\cdot

Q

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A\vphantom{\overline{A}}\mathstrut

\cdot

R

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{A}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

then by induction hypothesis and
definition

8

V_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=(\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)\cup\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,\overline{A}))\setminus\mathtt{names}(A);

the statement follows from the fact that
\mathtt{names}(A)=\mathtt{names}(\overline{A})
;

all other cases follow immediately from the induction hypothesis.
∎

Proof of
lemma

5
.

By structural induction on
P
. For the sake of brevity we let
P^{\prime}=\mathtt{inv}(P,A\lor B)
and omit at each step the shape of
P,P^{\prime}
: the interested reader may
inspect the corresponding steps in the proof of
lemma

1

(
appendix

0.C
). Because
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A,B)=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A\lor B)
, we have in any case
V_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}=V_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}
and it is
enough to show that
E_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}=E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}
:

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{C}\land\overline{D},A\lor B\}}
with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,\overline{C}\land\overline{D},A\lor B

where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{\overline{C}\land\overline{D}\}
, then by
definition

9

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=(\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,B}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C},A\}})\sqcup(\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{D},B\}})

and by
definition

6
we have

\displaystyle\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C},A\}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{D},B\}}

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C}\land\overline{D},A\lor B\}}=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket;

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}

with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,A\lor B,C,\overline{D}
where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{C,\overline{D}\}
, then by
definitions

9
and
6

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A,B}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A\lor B}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{\lor}
-rule application introducing
A\lor B

with premiss subtree
Q
, then
P^{\prime}=Q
and
\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket
;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{cut}
-rule application on formulas
C,\overline{C}
,
with premiss subderivations
Q,R
, we have by induction hypothesis
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(Q,A\lor B)}\rrbracket=\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket
and
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(R,A\lor B)}\rrbracket=\llbracket{R}\rrbracket
, hence

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(Q,A\lor B)}\rrbracket\odot_{C}\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(R,A\lor B)}\rrbracket=\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket\odot_{C}\llbracket{R}\rrbracket=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{sum}
-,
\mathtt{\lor}
- or
\mathtt{\land}
-rule
application that does not introduce
A\lor B
, with premiss subtrees
Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}
,
we have
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(Q_{i},A\lor B)}\rrbracket=\llbracket{Q_{i}}\rrbracket
by induction hypothesis
for all
1\leq i\leq n
: then

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(Q_{1},A\lor B)}\rrbracket\sqcup\ldots\sqcup\llbracket{\mathtt{inv}(Q_{n},A\lor B)}\rrbracket\\
=\llbracket{Q_{1}}\rrbracket\sqcup\ldots\sqcup\llbracket{Q_{n}}\rrbracket=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket.

∎

Proof of
lemma

6
.

We only prove the first part of the statement, i.e. that

\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A\land B)}\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket{P}\rrbracket{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A};

the argument for the second part is analogous. Let
P^{\prime}=\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A\land B)
,
As in the previous proof, we do not recall the shape of
P,P^{\prime}
; the reader is invited
to check our statements against the proofs of
lemmas

2
and
3
(
appendix

0.C
). Observe first that by

proposition

1
we have

V_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)=V_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}.

We then need to prove only that
E_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}\subseteq E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}
, as this
will be enough to guarantee that
E_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}\subseteq E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}
.
We proceed by structural induction on
P
:

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{C}\lor\overline{D},A\land B\}}
with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,\overline{C}\lor\overline{D},A\land B

where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{\overline{C}\lor\overline{D}\}
, then by
definitions

9
and
6

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,\overline{D}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C},A\}}\\
\sqsubseteq\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C},A\}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{D},B\}}=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{C}\lor\overline{D},A\land B\}}=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket;

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}

with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,A\land B,C,\overline{D}
where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{C,\overline{D}\}
, then by
definitions

9
and
6

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}\sqsubseteq\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A\land B}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}}=\llbracket{P}\rrbracket;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{\land}
-rule application introducing
A\land B

whose premiss subtrees
Q,R
have conclusions respectively
\thesis\Gamma,A

and
\thesis\Gamma,B
, then
P^{\prime}=Q
and the conclusion is immediate;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{cut}
-rule application on formulas
C,\overline{C}
,
with premiss subderivations
Q,R
, we have by induction hypothesis
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(Q,A\land B)}\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket
and
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(R,A\land B)}\rrbracket\sqsubseteq\llbracket{R}\rrbracket
, with

\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket=\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(Q,A\land B)}\rrbracket\odot_{C}\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(R,A\land B)}\rrbracket.

By
definition

8
,
xy\in E_{\llbracket{P^{\prime}}\rrbracket}
if and only if there is
an alternating path (
definition

7
) connecting
x
with
y

between
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(Q,A\land B)}\rrbracket
and
\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(R,A\land B)}\rrbracket

on inteface
\mathtt{names}(C)
. It is easy to check that the same sequence of vertices
is an alternating path between
\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket
and
\llbracket{R}\rrbracket
through interface
\mathtt{names}(C)
,
and therefore
xy\in E_{\llbracket{Q}\rrbracket\odot_{C}\llbracket{R}\rrbracket}=E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}
;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{sum}
-,
\mathtt{\lor}
- or
\mathtt{\land}
-rule
application that does not introduce
A\land B
, we conclude by induction hypothesis
and
proposition

7
. ∎

Proof of
proposition

2
.

Immediate by
lemma

5
when
A
is a
disjunction; for conjunctions we need to show that

\llbracket{P}\rrbracket=\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket\sqcup\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket,

whenever
P
is cut-free. In particular, it suffices to show that

E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket}\cup E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket}.

By structural induction on
P
, assuming
A=A_{1}\land A_{2}
:

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2},A\}}
with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2},A

where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2}\}
, then

\displaystyle\llbracket{P}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2},A\}}=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{1},A_{1}\}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\}},

\displaystyle\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,\overline{B}_{2}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{1},A_{1}\}},

\displaystyle\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\}}.

Because the weakening graphs have no edges, we can conclude that

E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=E_{\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{1},A_{1}\}}}\sqcup E_{\mathtt{Id}_{\{\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\}}}=E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket}\sqcup E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket}.

•

if
P
ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{B,\overline{C}\}}

with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,A,B,\overline{C}
where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{B,\overline{C}\}
,
then we have

\displaystyle\llbracket{P}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{B,\overline{C}\}},

\displaystyle\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A_{1}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{B,\overline{C}\}},

\displaystyle\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket=\mathtt{Wk}_{\Delta,A_{2}}\sqcup\mathtt{Id}_{\{B,\overline{C}\}}.

Therefore, because the weakening graphs have no edges,

E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=E_{\mathtt{Id}_{\{B,\overline{C}\}}}=E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(P,A)}\rrbracket}=E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(P,A)}\rrbracket},

from which the conclusion follows.

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{\land}
-rule application introducing
A
,
the conclusion is trivial as
P=\mathtt{isl}(P,A)
;

•

if
P
ends with a
\mathtt{\sqcup}
-,
\mathtt{\lor}
- or
\mathtt{\land}
-rule
application that does not introduce
A
, with premiss subtrees
Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}
,
we have by induction hypothesis

E_{\llbracket{Q_{i}}\rrbracket}=E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(Q_{i},A)}\rrbracket}\cup E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(Q_{i},A)}\rrbracket}.

for all
1\leq i\leq n
. The result then follows from the fact that

E_{\llbracket{P}\rrbracket}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}E_{\llbracket{Q_{i}}\rrbracket}=\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{l}}(Q_{i},A)}\rrbracket}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}E_{\llbracket{\mathtt{inv_{r}}(Q_{i},A)}\rrbracket}\right).\qed

Appendix 0.F
Proofs of lemmas regarding branch-labeled axiom graphs

0.F.1
Properties of branch sets

Lemma 22

For all named formulas
A
, if
X\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
then
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(A)
.

Proof.

Immediate by induction on
A
.
∎

Proof of
lemma

7
.

Observe first that
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma}\mathtt{names}(A)
,
and assume
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
. By definition
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
,
therefore
X=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma}(X\cap\mathtt{names}(A))
; we know also that

(X\cap\mathtt{names}(A))\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
for all
A\in\Gamma
, hence we can
choose
X_{A}=X\cap\mathtt{names}(A)
.

Conversely, assume
X=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma}X_{A}
with
X_{A}\in\mathtt{Br}(A)

for all
A\in\Gamma
. By
lemma

22
,
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(A)
;
moreover, because
\Gamma
is sharing-free, its elements have pairwise disjoint name
sets, hence the
X_{A}
in particular are pairwise disjoint and
X\cap\mathtt{names}(A)=X_{A}\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
, as desired.
∎

Proof of
lemma

8
.

Assume
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma\cup\Delta)
: by
lemma

7
there
is an indexed family
(X_{A})_{A\in\Gamma\cup\Delta}
of name sets such that
X=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma\cup\Delta}X_{A}
and
X_{A}\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
for all
A\in\Gamma\cup\Delta
. Let then
Y=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma}X_{A}
and
Z=\bigcup_{A\in\Delta}X_{A}
: again by
lemma

7
,
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
and
Z\in\mathtt{Br}(\Delta)
, and obviously
X=Y\cup Z
. The argument for the converse is
analogous, reversing the direction of all implications.
∎

Proof of
proposition

3
.

Fact (i) is left to the reader. For fact (ii), observe that
\mathtt{Br}(\{A,B\})=\mathtt{Br}(\{A\}\cup\{B\})=\mathtt{Br}(A\lor B)
as an immediate consequence of

lemma

8
: then we have

\displaystyle\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\lor B)

\displaystyle=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A\lor B)\}

\displaystyle=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\{A,B\})\}

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A,B).

For fact (iii), recall that
\mathtt{Br}(A\land B)=\mathtt{Br}(A)\cup\mathtt{Br}(B)
;
then, again by
lemma

8
,

\displaystyle\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\land B)

\displaystyle=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A\land B)\}

\displaystyle=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A)\cup\mathtt{Br}(B)\}

\displaystyle=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A)\}

\displaystyle\qquad\cup\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(B)\}

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)\cup\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B).

For fact (iv), observe that (by an easy inductive argument) all branches of
A

(resp. of
B
) must be non-empty, and remember that
\Gamma,A,B
have disjoint
name sets by hypothesis. Let then
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)\cap\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
:
by
lemma

8
there is a
non-empty

Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A)

such that
Y\subseteq X
. By construction we have also
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B)
, but then there should be some name
z\in Y\subseteq\mathtt{names}(A)

such that
z\in\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B)
, which is impossible.
∎

0.F.2
Properties of branch-labeled axiom graphs

Lemma 23

For all bl-graphs
G
,

\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(G))=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(G),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)\}.

Proof.

Immediate, see
definition

14
.
∎

Lemma 24

For any pair
A,\overline{B}
of disjoint and sharing-free named formulas such that

A\equiv B
,
\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}})=\mathtt{Br}(A,\overline{B})
.

Proof.

By induction on the height of
A
:

•

if
A
is atomic, then
\mathtt{Br}(A,\overline{B})=\{\mathtt{names}(A,\overline{B})\}=\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}})
by
propositions

3
and
14
;

•

if
A=A_{1}\lor A_{2}
and
\overline{B}=\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2}
, then
by
definition

14

\displaystyle\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}})

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{2}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{1},\overline{B}_{1}\}})\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{1}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}\}}))

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{2}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{1},\overline{B}_{1}\}}))\cup\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{1}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}\}})).

By induction hypothesis,
\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{1},\overline{B}_{1}\}})=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},\overline{B}_{1})

and
\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}\}})=\mathtt{Br}(A_{2},\overline{B}_{2})
;
by
lemmas

23
and
8

\displaystyle\begin{multlined}\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{2}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{1},\overline{B}_{1}\}}))\\
=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},\overline{B}_{1}),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A_{2})\}=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B}_{1}),\end{multlined}

\displaystyle\begin{multlined}\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A_{1}}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}\}}))\\
=\{X\cup Y\mid X\in\mathtt{Br}(A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}),Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A_{1})\}=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B}_{2}).\end{multlined}

Then, again by
proposition

3
,

\displaystyle\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}})

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B}_{1})\cup\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B}_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Br}(A_{1}\lor A_{2},\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2})=\mathtt{Br}(A,\overline{B}).\qed

Corollary 8

Let
\Gamma
be any sharing-free set of named formulas,
A,\overline{B}
a pair of
disjoint and sharing free named formulas that share no names with
\Gamma
and
such that
A\equiv B
: then

\mathtt{Br}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{A,\overline{B}\}}))=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A,\overline{B}).

Proof of
proposition

4
.

The proof that
V_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
is analogous to that of

proposition

1
and left to the reader. We prove by structural
induction on
P
that
\mathtt{Br}(\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis)\subseteq\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
:

•

if
P
is an axiom rule application, the conclusion follows immediately
from
corollary

8
;

•

if
P
has the form

\cdot

Q

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A\vphantom{\overline{A}}\mathstrut

\cdot

R

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{A}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

then by
definition

13
, if
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis\odot_{A}\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis)

there is either
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis)
or
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis)

such that
X=Y\setminus\mathtt{names}(A)
. By induction hypothesis we have either

Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
or
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,\overline{A})
, hence

X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
by
corollary

3
;

all other cases follow immediately from the induction hypothesis.
∎

0.F.3
Behaviour under inversion

Lemma 25

For all bl-graphs
G,H
and sharing-free sets
\Gamma
of named formulas,

\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(G\sqcup H)=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(G)\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(H).

Proof.

Left to the reader.
∎

Lemma 26

For all bl-graphs
G
and sharing-free sets
\Gamma\cup\Delta
of named formulas,

\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(G))=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma\cup\Delta}(G).

Proof.

The identity is obvious for vertices. For the edge-branch relation, let

e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(G))}X
: there are then
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(G)
,

Z\in\mathtt{Br}(\Delta)
and
W\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
such that
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}Y

and
X=Y\cup Z\cup W
. By
lemma

8
,
Z\cup W\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma\cup\Delta)
, hence
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma\cup\Delta}(G)}X
.
Conversely, let
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma\cup\Delta}(G)}X
: there are
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(G)
,
Z\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma\cup\Delta)
such that
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}Y

and
X=Y\cup Z
. Again by
lemma

8
,
Z=Z^{\prime}\cup Z^{\prime\prime}

for some
Z^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma),Z^{\prime\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(\Delta)
, hence
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Gamma}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(G))}X
.
∎

Proof of
lemma

10
.

Almost identical to the proof of
lemma

5

(
appendix

0.E
); only the base case is different (axioms).
Let
P^{\prime}
denote the inverted derivation
\mathtt{inv}(P,A\lor B)
; then:

•

if

ends with an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{C}\land\overline{D},A\lor B\}}

, then by

we have

\displaystyle\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{C}\land\overline{D},A\lor B\}}),

\displaystyle\llparenthesis{P^{\prime}}\rrparenthesis=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{C},A\}})\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,A}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{D},B\}}),

and by

\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{C},A\}})\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{D},B\}})).

We apply

to get

\displaystyle\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{C},A\}}))\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta}(\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{A}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{D},B\}}))

\displaystyle=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{C},A\}})\sqcup\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,A}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{\overline{D},B\}})=\llparenthesis{P^{\prime}}\rrparenthesis.

\llparenthesis{P^{\prime}}\rrparenthesis=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,A,B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}})=\mathtt{Wk}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\Delta,A\lor B}(\mathtt{Id}^{\mathtt{bl}}_{\{C,\overline{D}\}})=\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis.\qed

Lemma 27

For all bl-graphs
G\sqsubseteq H
and name sets
X\subseteq\mathcal{N}
,

V_{G}\subseteq X\implies G\sqsubseteq H{\upharpoonright}_{X}.

Proof.

If
V_{G}\subseteq X
then obviously
V_{G}\subseteq V_{H{\upharpoonright}_{X}}=(V_{H}\cap X)
.
Moreover, let
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}Y
: we have
Y\subseteq V_{G}\subseteq X
by
definition

11

and we know by hypothesis that
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{H}Y
, hence
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{H{\upharpoonright}_{X}}Y
.
∎

Lemma 28

Let
\Gamma\cup\{A\land B\}
be a sharing-free set of named formulas,
G

any bl-graph with
\mathtt{Br}(G)\subseteq\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\land B)
: then

\mathtt{Br}(G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A})\subseteq\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)\text{ and }\mathtt{Br}(G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B})\subseteq\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B).

Proof.

We only prove the first half of the statement, the second half is similar. Observe
that (by an easy inductive argument) every branch of
B
is non-empty, and remember
that
\Gamma,A,B
have disjoint name sets. Let
X\in\mathtt{Br}(G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A})

and assume
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
: by
lemma

8
there
are
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
and a
non-empty

Z\in\mathtt{Br}(B)
such that

X=Y\cup Z
. However, we have
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
by construction,
hence
Z\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
, which is disjoint from
\mathtt{names}(B)
,
a contradiction. Therefore
X\notin\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
, and by exclusion we
have
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
.
∎

.

Proof of
lemma

12
.

Observe first that

\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A\land B)=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)\cup\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B),

hence

V_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A\land B)=V_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}\cup V_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}.

For the branch-label relation, we start by recalling the fact that

\mathtt{Br}(\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis)\subseteq\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\land B)=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)\cup\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B).

Now let
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis}X
: if
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
, then in particular

X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
, hence
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}X
;
similarly, if
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
then
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}X
.
We have then

\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis\sqsubseteq{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}\sqcup{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}};

the reverse inclusion is immediate.
∎

0.F.4
Auxiliary lemmas for cut-elimination

Proof of
lemma

13
.

By structural induction on
P
; we leave the base case (axioms),
superpositions and the logical rules to the reader. For cuts, assume
P

has the form

\cdot

Q

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,A\vphantom{\overline{A}}\mathstrut

\cdot

R

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma,\overline{A}\mathstrut

\mathtt{cut}

\displaystyle\thesis\Gamma\mathstrut

We have then
\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis=\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis\odot_{A}\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis
. Let
xy\in E_{\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis}
:
there is by
definition

13
a labeled alternating path
z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}

between
\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis
and
\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis
through the interface
\mathtt{names}(A)
,
with
xy=z_{1}z_{n}
. For all
1<i<n
(the interface nodes) we have
\overline{A}[z_{i}]=\overline{A[z_{i}]}
. Let
\alpha=\Gamma[x]
. There are two possibilities:

•

odd edges in
\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis
, even edges in
\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis
:
we prove
by secondary induction on
i
that for all
1<i<n
, if
i
is odd then

A[z_{i}]=\alpha
, if it is even then
A[z_{i}]=\overline{\alpha}
. If
i=2

(even) then
z_{1}z_{2}\in E_{\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis}
, hence by the primary induction hypothesis

A[z_{2}]=(\Gamma,A)[z_{2}]=\overline{(\Gamma,A)[z_{1}]}=\overline{\Gamma[z_{1}]}=\overline{\Gamma[x]}=\overline{\alpha}.

If
i>2
and even, then
z_{i-1}z_{i}\in E_{\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis}
; by the secondary
induction hypothesis
A[z_{i-1}]=\alpha
, and by the primary hypothesis

A[z_{i}]=(\Gamma,A)[z_{i}]=\overline{(\Gamma,A)[z_{i-1}]}=\overline{A[z_{i-1}]}=\overline{\alpha}.

If
i>2
and odd, then
z_{i-1}z_{i}\in E_{\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis}
; by the secondary
induction hypothesis
A[z_{i-1}]=\overline{\alpha}
hence
\overline{A}[z_{i-1}]=\alpha
;
by the primary hypothesis

\overline{A}[z_{i}]=(\Gamma,\overline{A})[z_{i}]=\overline{(\Gamma,\overline{A})[z_{i-1}]}=\overline{\overline{A}[z_{i-1}]}=\overline{\alpha},

therefore
A[z_{i}]=\overline{\overline{\alpha}}=\alpha
. We conclude by cases on
n
:
if
n=2
, then by the primary induction hypothesis

\Gamma[y]=(\Gamma,A)[z_{2}]=\overline{(\Gamma,A)[z_{1}]}=\overline{\Gamma[x]};

if
n>2
and even, then
z_{n-1}z_{n}\in E_{\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis}
and
A[z_{n-1}]=\alpha
; by the primary induction hypothesis

\Gamma[y]=(\Gamma,A)[z_{n}]=\overline{(\Gamma,A)[z_{n-1}]}=\overline{A[z_{n-1}]}=\overline{\alpha}=\overline{\Gamma[x]};

if
n>2
and odd, then
z_{n-1}z_{n}\in E_{\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis}
and
A[z_{n-1}]=\overline{\alpha}
, hence
\overline{A}[z_{n-1}]=\alpha
; by the primary induction hypothesis

\Gamma[y]=(\Gamma,\overline{A})[z_{n}]=\overline{(\Gamma,\overline{A})[z_{n-1}]}=\overline{\overline{A}[z_{n-1}]}=\overline{\alpha}=\overline{\Gamma[x]}.

•

odd edges in
\llparenthesis{R}\rrparenthesis
, even edges in
\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis
:
we proceed as
in the previous case, swapping
Q
with
R
and
A
with
\overline{A}
. ∎

Proof of
lemma

16
.

By structural induction on
P
. We prove the result only for the base case (i.e. the
axioms), all other cases are more or less immediate.

Case (i).

P
is an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B},A\}}

with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,\overline{B},A
, where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{\overline{B}\}
:

•

if
A=A_{1}\lor A_{2}
is a disjunction, then
\mathtt{inv}(P,A)
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B}_{1},A_{1}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},A_{1},A_{2}\mathstrut

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2}\mathstrut

\mathtt{\land}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2}\mathstrut

\mathtt{\lor}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}\lor A_{2}\mathstrut

where
\overline{B}=\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2}
. We have

\displaystyle\mathtt{vh}(P)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}\lor A_{2})

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta)

\displaystyle\qquad\!+1+\mathtt{deg}(\overline{B}_{1})+\mathtt{deg}(\overline{B}_{2})

\displaystyle\qquad\!+1+\mathtt{deg}(A_{1})+\mathtt{deg}(A_{2})

\displaystyle=3+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2})

and

\displaystyle\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))

\displaystyle=2+\max\{1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},A_{1},A_{2}),1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2})\}

\displaystyle=3+\max\{\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},A_{1},A_{2}),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2})\}.

Clearly,

\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},A_{1},A_{2}),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2})\leq\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2}),

hence
\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))\leq\mathtt{vh}(P)
;

•

if
A=A_{1}\land A_{2}
is a conjunction, then
\mathtt{inv}(P,A)
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B}_{1},A_{1}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}\mathstrut

\mathtt{\lor}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}\mathstrut

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\mathstrut

\mathtt{\lor}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2},A_{2}\mathstrut

\mathtt{\land}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1}\land\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}\lor A_{2}\mathstrut

where
\overline{B}=\overline{B}_{1}\lor\overline{B}_{2}
. We have as before

\mathtt{vh}(P)=3+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2})

and

\displaystyle\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))

\displaystyle=1+\max\{2+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}),2+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{2})\}

\displaystyle=3+\max\{\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{2})\},

with

\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1}),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{2})\leq\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B}_{1},\overline{B}_{2},A_{1},A_{2}),

and again
\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))\leq\mathtt{vh}(P)
.

Case (ii).

P
is an axiom rule application of the kind
\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B},C\}}

with conclusion
\thesis\Delta,A,\overline{B},C
, where
\Gamma=\Delta\cup\{\overline{B},C\}
:

•

if
A=A_{1}\lor A_{2}
is a disjunction, then
\mathtt{inv}(P,A)
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B},C\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B},C\mathstrut

\mathtt{\lor}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A_{1}\lor A_{2},\overline{B},C\mathstrut

We have

\displaystyle\mathtt{vh}(P)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1}\lor A_{2},\overline{B},C)

\displaystyle=1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,\overline{B},C)

\displaystyle\qquad\!+1+\mathtt{deg}(A_{1})+\mathtt{deg}(A_{2})

\displaystyle=2+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B},C)

and

\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))=2+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B},C),

hence
a fortiori

\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))\leq\mathtt{vh}(P)
;

•

if
A=A_{1}\land A_{2}
is a conjunction, then
\mathtt{inv}(P,A)
has the form

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B},C\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A_{1},\overline{B},C\mathstrut

\mathtt{ax}_{\{\overline{B},C\}}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A_{2},\overline{B},C\mathstrut

\mathtt{\land}

\displaystyle\thesis\Delta,A_{1}\land A_{2},\overline{B},C\mathstrut

We have as before

\mathtt{vh}(P)=2+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B},C)

and

\displaystyle\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))

\displaystyle=1+\max\{1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},\overline{B},C),1+\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{2},\overline{B},C)\}

\displaystyle=2+\max\{\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},\overline{B},C),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{2},\overline{B},C)\}

with

\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},\overline{B},C),\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{2},\overline{B},C)\leq\mathtt{deg}(\thesis\Delta,A_{1},A_{2},\overline{B},C)

hence
\mathtt{vh}(\mathtt{inv}(P,A))\leq\mathtt{vh}(P)
. ∎

Appendix 0.G
Proof of the semantic cut-admissibility lemma

We devote the present section to the proof of
lemma

14
,
which requires a somewhat involved construction. We start by fixing a set

\mathtt{Pol}=\{{\circ},{\bullet}\}

of
polarities
. For
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
, we write
\overline{p}
for the opposite
polarity, i.e. let
\overline{\circ}={\bullet}
and
\overline{\bullet}={\circ}
. As background
data for the construction, we have to provide a pair of bl-graphs
G_{\circ},G_{\bullet}

and a
finite
set of names
I\subseteq\mathcal{N}
to act as the composition
interface. The two graphs are required to satisfy the following property:

there is a unique branch name
X\subseteq\mathcal{N}
such that, for all
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
and
e\in E_{G_{p}}
,
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G_{p}}^{I}X
;

in other words, the two graphs must have collectively a unique branch up to names in
the interface. The restriction has two important consequences:

•

all alternating paths between the two graphs through
I
are necessarily

X
-labeled, hence composable;

•

any edge can be added to any alternating path, without caring for its label.

More formally, let
z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}
be an
X
-labeled alternating path between

G_{\circ}
and
G_{\bullet}
through interface
I
(
definition

12
).
For any
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
we call the path

•

p
-initial
, if all odd edges are in
G_{p}
and all even edges in
G_{\overline{p}}
;

•

p
-final
, if it is
p
-initial with even
n
, or
\overline{p}
-initial
with odd
n
.

Because the graphs and interface – as well as the unique branch label – are fixed, from now
on we are going to speak simply of alternating paths, without mentioning the full expression
(
X
-labeled alt. paths between
G_{\circ}
and
G_{\bullet}
through interface
I
).
The following properties hold:

Lemma 29

For all
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
and edge
xy\in E_{G_{p}}
,
x,y
is a
p
-initial
and
p
-final alternating path.

Lemma 30

For any
p,q\in\mathtt{Pol}
, if
z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}
is a
p
-initial and

q
-final alternating path then
z_{n},\ldots,z_{1}
is a
q
-initial and
p
-final
alternating path.

Lemma 31

Let
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
, and let
\vec{z}=z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}
,
\vec{w}=w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}
be alternating paths such that
\vec{z}
is
p
-final,

\vec{w}
is
\overline{p}
-initial and
z_{n}=w_{1}
: then

\vec{zw}=z_{1},\ldots,(z_{n}=w_{1}),\ldots,w_{n}

is also an alternating path,
q
-initial iff so is
\vec{z}
and
q
-final
iff so is
\vec{w}
.

The proofs are tedious but straightforward and we leave them to the interested reader.
The construction operates on
finite
sets
\sigma
of pairs with each pair of
the form

\langle S,(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})\rangle\in\sigma

where
S\subseteq I\times\mathtt{Pol}
is a
set of name-polarity pairs
(with names
from the interface
I
) and
v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in(V_{G_{\circ}}\cup V_{G_{\bullet}})^{\ast}

is a
finite sequence of vertices
from the two graphs. We call
\sigma
a
state

of the construction. We distinguish
consistent
and
live
states based on
certain sets of local and global properties, respectively:

Definition 28

(Consistency)
.

Call a state
\sigma
of the construction
consistent
if and only if all
pairs
\langle S,(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})\rangle\in\sigma
satisfy the following conditions:

1.

mutual exclusion:
at most one polarity is assigned to each name in
S
,
i.e. for all
(x,p),(y,q)\in S
,
x=y
implies
p=q
; equivalently,
if
(x,p)\in S
then
(x,\overline{p})\notin S
.

2.

alternation:

v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}
is an alternating path;

3.

inclusion:
if
v_{1}\in I
(resp.
v_{n}\in I
), then there is

p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that
(v_{1},p)\in S
(resp.
(v_{n},p)\in S
);

4.

coloring:
if
(v_{1},p)\in S
(resp.
(v_{n},p)\in S
), then
the alternating path
v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}
is
p
-initial (resp.
p
-final).

Consider now two sets
S,T\subseteq I\times\mathtt{Pol}
of name-polarity pairs.
We say that
S,T

compose on name
x\in\mathcal{N}
(notation
S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x}}{{\bowtie}}T
)
iff there is a polarity
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that
(x,p)\in S
,
(x,\overline{p})\in T

and
S\setminus\{(x,p)\}=T\setminus\{(x,\overline{p})\}
.

Definition 29

(Liveness)
.

Call a state
\sigma
of the construction
live
iff it is non-empty and,
for all
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
and
(x,p)\in S
, there is

\langle T,\vec{w}\rangle\in\sigma
such that
S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x}}{{\bowtie}}T
.

Now let us define for any state
\sigma
the set of
live names of
\sigma
:

\mathtt{names}(\sigma)=\{x\in\mathcal{N}\mid\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma,(x,p)\in S\}.

Definition 30

(Terminal state)
.

Call a state
\sigma
of the construction
terminal
iff for all
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
,
S
is empty; equivalently iff
\mathtt{names}(\sigma)=\emptyset
.

Lemma 32

Let
\sigma
be any consistent, live and terminal state: there is a pair
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
such that
\vec{z}
is a complete alternating
path.

Proof.

By liveness
\sigma
is non-empty, i.e. there is at least one pair
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
. Let
\vec{z}=z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}
and assume
z_{1}\in I
:
by the inclusion condition (consistency) there should be
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that

(z_{1},p)\in S
, against the hypothesis that
\sigma
be terminal, hence
z_{1}\notin I
.
The same argument shows that
z_{n}\notin I
.
∎

Corollary 9

If there is a consistent, live and terminal state, then there is a complete
X
-labeled
alternating path between
G_{\circ}
and
G_{\bullet}
through interface
I
.

Corollary 10

If there is a consistent, live and terminal state, then the composite bl-graph
G_{\circ}\odot_{I}G_{\bullet}
has at least one edge.

We come now to the key lemma of this proof, showing that every consistent and live state
can be transformed into a consistent, live and terminal one in a finite number of steps.
Thus we reduce the problem of showing that the composite graph is non-empty to that of
constructing a consistent and live state.

Lemma 33

(Reduction lemma)

For any consistent and live state
\sigma
such that
\mathtt{names}(\sigma)

is non-empty, there is a consistent and live state
\tau
such that

\mathtt{names}(\tau)\subsetneq\mathtt{names}(\sigma).

Because the interface
I
is finite by assumption, the set of live names of any state
must be finite, therefore we can reach a terminal one by iterating the reduction lemma
finitely many times:

Corollary 11

If there is a consistent and live state, then there is a consistent, live and terminal state.

Corollary 12

If there is a consistent and live state, then the composite bl-graph
G_{\circ}\odot_{I}G_{\bullet}
has at least one edge.

Proof of the reduction lemma.

By assumption there is
x\in\mathtt{names}(\sigma)
. We associate to every pair

\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
a new pair
\langle S^{\prime},\vec{z}^{\prime}\rangle

constructed as follows, while simultaneously proving that the new pair satisfies all
consistency conditions (
definition

28
):

•

if there is no
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that
(x,p)\in S
, then let

S^{\prime}=S
,
\vec{z}^{\prime}=\vec{z}
; all consistency conditions are clearly preserved;

•

otherwise let
\langle T,\vec{w}\rangle\in\sigma
be the pair
such that
S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x}}{{\bowtie}}T
, whose existence is guaranteed by liveness:
we have
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that
(x,p)\in S
and
(x,\overline{p})\in T
;

•

let
S^{\prime}=S\setminus\{(x,p)\}=T\setminus\{(x,\overline{p})\}
; since we
are just removing one pair, mutual exclusion is preserved;

•

let
\vec{z}=z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}
and
\vec{w}=w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}
;

•

if both
z_{1},z_{n}\neq x
, then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=\vec{z}
; the last three
consistency conditions are preserved because no endpoint is
x
;

•

if on the other hand
w_{1},w_{n}\neq x
, then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=\vec{w}
;
the last three consistency conditions are preserved because no endpoint is
x

and
S^{\prime}=T\setminus\{(x,\overline{p})\}
;

•

otherwise there are four mutually exclusive cases:

–

if
z_{n}=x,w_{1}=x
then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=z_{1},\ldots,(z_{n}=w_{1}),\ldots,w_{n}
;

–

if
z_{n}=x,w_{n}=x
then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=z_{1},\ldots,(z_{n}=w_{n}),\ldots,w_{1}
;

–

if
z_{1}=x,w_{1}=x
then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=z_{n},\ldots,(z_{1}=w_{1}),\ldots,w_{n}
;

–

if
z_{1}=x,w_{n}=x
then let
\vec{z}^{\prime}=z_{n},\ldots,(z_{1}=w_{n}),\ldots,w_{1}
.

For the inclusion condition, observe that no repetition of vertices is allowed in
an alternating path; because the endpoint
x
has become internal in
\vec{z}^{\prime}
,
inclusion must still hold for the other endpoints. For alternation:
\vec{z}^{\prime}
is
obtained by joining two sequences on
x
, after possibly reversing them. Reversal
preserves alternating paths by
lemma

30
; the composition is
correct (
lemma

31
) because the two original pairs satisfy
the coloring condition, hence the first half is
p
-final and the second half
is
\overline{p}
-initial. Finally, the coloring condition is preserved because the
endpoints preserve their original initiality and finality by
lemmas

30
and
31
.

Clearly the construction is performed in such a way that for any
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
, there is no
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
such that
(x,p)\in S^{\prime}
. We define
then
\tau
as

\tau=\{\langle S^{\prime},\vec{z}^{\prime}\rangle\mid\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma\}.

Since
\sigma
is finite, so is
\tau
, hence it is a consistent state. We have obviously

\mathtt{names}(\tau)\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\sigma)

and from what we said above we known that
x\notin\mathtt{names}(\tau)
, hence the
inclusion is strict, as required.

We have now to show that
\tau
is live (
definition

29
). It must be non-empty
because so is
\sigma
; let then
\langle S^{\prime},\vec{z}^{\prime}\rangle\in\tau
and
(y,p)\in S^{\prime}
: by construction there is some pair
\langle S,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma

such that
S^{\prime}=S\setminus\{(x,q)\}
, and by the liveness of
\sigma
there is
another pair
\langle T,\vec{w}\rangle\in\sigma
such that
S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y}}{{\bowtie}}T
. Then there is a pair
\langle T^{\prime},\vec{w}^{\prime}\rangle\in\tau
such that
T^{\prime}=T\setminus\{(x,\overline{q})\}
, and we have
S^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y}}{{\bowtie}}T^{\prime}
: remembering
that
y\neq x
,

•

(y,p)\in(S\setminus\{(x,q)\})=S^{\prime}
;

•

(y,\overline{p})\in(T\setminus\{(x,\overline{q})\})=T^{\prime}
;

•

S^{\prime}\setminus\{(y,p)\}=(S\setminus\{(y,p)\})\setminus\{(x,q)\}\\
\hbox{}\qquad\qquad=(T\setminus\{(y,\overline{p})\})\setminus\{(x,\overline{q})\}=T^{\prime}\setminus\{(y,\overline{p})\}
. ∎

As announced above, we complete the proof of
lemma

14
by
showing that a consistent and live state can be constructed. We start with an auxiliary
lemma:

Lemma 34

For any sharing-free named formula
A
and function

f:\mathtt{names}(A)\to\mathtt{Pol}

there is either
X\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
such that
fX=\{{\circ}\}
or
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{A})
such that
fY=\{{\bullet}\}
.

Proof.

By induction on
A
. If
A={\alpha}^{x}
then
\mathtt{Br}(A)=\mathtt{Br}(\overline{A})=\{{x}\}
, and necessarily either
f\{x\}=\{{\circ}\}
or
f\{x\}=\{{\bullet}\}
.

If
A=B\land C
(with
\overline{A}=\overline{B}\lor\overline{C}
) then
\mathtt{Br}(A)=\mathtt{Br}(B)\cup\mathtt{Br}(C)
). By induction hypothesis there is either
X^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(B)
such that
fX^{\prime}=\{{\circ}\}
or
Y^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{B})

such that
fY^{\prime}=\{{\bullet}\}
. In the first case, let
X=X^{\prime}
and we’re done.
Otherwise, there is again by induction hypothesis either
X^{\prime\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(C)

s.t.
fX^{\prime\prime}=\{{\circ}\}
, or
Y^{\prime\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{C})
s.t.
fY^{\prime\prime}=\{{\bullet}\}
.
If there is such a
X^{\prime\prime}
, let
X=X^{\prime\prime}
; otherwise, let
Y=Y^{\prime}\cup Y^{\prime\prime}\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{B}\lor\overline{C})
: we have
fY=fY^{\prime}\cup fY^{\prime\prime}=\{{\bullet}\}
.

If
A=B\lor C
, apply the same argument, swapping polarities and
A
with
\overline{A}
.
∎

Proof of
lemma

14
.

We fix
G_{\circ}=\llparenthesis{P}\rrparenthesis
,
G_{\bullet}=\llparenthesis{Q}\rrparenthesis
and
I=\mathtt{names}(A)
.

I
is obviously finite, and because the context of the conclusions of
P,Q
is
atomic by hypothesis, the condition about branches is satisfied too (the unique branch
name
X
is the unique one in
\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
, i.e.
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
).

We construct a state
\sigma
as follows:

\sigma=\{\langle f,(x,y)\rangle\mid f\in\mathtt{Pol}^{I},p\in\mathtt{Pol},xy\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G_{p}}X\cup Y,fY=\{p\}\}.

Let us unpack the construction first, then we shall prove that the state is consistent
and live.
\mathtt{Pol}^{I}
is the set of all functions from
I=\mathtt{names}(A)

to
\mathtt{Pol}
seen as sets of pairs, i.e.
\mathtt{Pol}^{I}\subseteq I\times\mathtt{Pol}
;
we pair each
f\in\mathtt{Pol}^{I}
with any finite sequence
x,y
of vertices
such that, for at least one polarity
p\in\mathtt{Pol}
,
xy
is an edge in
G_{p}
,
and moreover one of its branch labels satisfies the following conditions:

•

it is equal to
X\cup Y
for some
Y
(where
X
is the unique branch
name of
\Gamma
described above);

•

it is such that
fY=\{p\}
.

\sigma
is clearly finite, hence a state. For consistency (
definition

28
),
let
\langle f,(x,y)\rangle\in\sigma
:

•

mutual exclusion:
this condition can be read as asking that
f

be the graph of a function, hence it is obviously satisfied;

•

alternation:

xy
is an edge in either
G_{\circ}
or
G_{\bullet}

by construction, hence an alternating path by
lemma

29
;

•

inclusion:
because
f
is total, if
x\in I
then
(x,fx)\in f
,
and similarly for
y
;

•

coloring:
let
(x,p)\in f
; by construction there is
q\in\mathtt{Pol}
,
Y\in\mathcal{N}
such that
xy\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G_{q}}X\cup Y
with

fY=\{q\}
. By
lemma

8
, every branch name of
G_{q}

is the union of the unique branch name
X
of
\Gamma
with some branch name
of either
A
(if
q={\circ}
) or
\overline{A}
(if
q={\bullet}
).
If
q={\circ}
, then,
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
, otherwise
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{A})
.
By
definition

11

x\in X\cup Y
, and because
x\in I
we must
have
x\in Y
. We know that
fY=\{q\}
, hence in particular
p=f(x)=q
.
The path
x,y
is obviously
q
-initial, hence
p
-initial. Analogous reasoning
shows that if
(y,p^{\prime})\in f
, then the path is
p^{\prime}
-final.

For liveness (
definition

29
) we argue first that
\sigma
is non-empty:
by
lemma

34
above, there is for each
f\in\mathtt{Pol}^{I}
at least one branch
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(A)
with
fY=\{{\circ}\}

or
Y\in\mathtt{Br}(\overline{A})
with
fY=\{{\bullet}\}
. Let
fY=\{p\}
;
by
lemma

17
,
(X\cup Y)\in\mathtt{Br}(G_{p})
,
i.e. there is
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G_{p}}X\cup Y
. We have thus proven not just that
\sigma

is non-empty, but also that for each
f\in\mathtt{Pol}^{I}
there is at least one
pair
\langle f,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
.

Now let
\langle f,\vec{z}\rangle\in\sigma
,
(x,p)\in f
; by inverting the polarity
assignment of
x
in
f
we obtain
f^{\prime}=(f\setminus\{(x,p)\})\cup\{(x,\overline{p})\}\in\mathtt{Pol}^{I}
. By the reasoning above there is
\langle f^{\prime},\vec{w}\rangle\in\sigma
,
and it is immediate by construction that
f\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x}}{{\bowtie}}f^{\prime}
.
∎

Appendix 0.H
Totality lemmas and correctness algorithm for BLG

Proof of
lemma

17
.

By structural induction on
P
. If
P
ends with an axiom rule application,
the conclusion is equivalent to
corollary

8
; if
P
ends with
a superposition rule application, it follows immediately from the induction hypothesis;
if
P
ends with a logical rule, we conclude from the induction hypothesis and

proposition

3
, points (ii) and (iii). The details
are left to the reader.
∎

Proof of
lemma

18
.

We have
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A,B)=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A\lor B)
;
\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A,B)=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\lor B)
by
proposition

3
;
and finally
(\Gamma,A,B)[x]=(\Gamma,A\lor B)[x]
for all
x\in\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A,B)
.
∎

Proof of
lemma

19
.

We have two prove two facts:
(i)
that
G
is effectively equal to the union
of the two restrictions, and
(ii)
that the two restrictions are total w.r.t. the
restricted conclusions. For fact (i), we have obviously

\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A\land B)=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)\cup\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B).

Then by construction
V_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
and

V_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B)
, hence
V_{G}=V_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}\cup V_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}
. Now let
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}X
. By totality
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A\land B)
; then by
proposition

3
either
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
or
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
: in the first case we have

X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
hence
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}X
;
similarly in the second case we have
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}X
. The reverse
inclusion is obvious.

For fact (ii), we have already argued that the two restriction have the appropriate vertex
sets (
definition

17
, point (i)); that all edges link dual atoms (
definition

17
,
point (iii)) follows from the fact that the edges come from
G
, which satisfies the same
condition, and for all
x\in\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)
(resp.
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B)
)
we have
(\Gamma,A\land B)[x]=(\Gamma,A)[x]
(resp.
(\Gamma,B)[x]
). Finally
we have to show that
\mathtt{Br}(G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A})=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
and

\mathtt{Br}(G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B})=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
(
definition

17
, point (ii)).
The forward inclusions are proved already in
lemma

28
.
For the reverse, let
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,A)
(resp.
\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma,B)
);
by totality there is
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}X
, and because
X\subseteq\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,A)

(resp.
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma,B)
) we have
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,A}}X
(resp.
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G{\upharpoonright}_{\Gamma,B}}X
).
∎

0.H.1
Correctness algorithm for BLG

Proof of
proposition

5
.

We work under the reasonable assumption that checking name equality requires constant time.
Let us start by recalling the definition of the size of
\mathbf{G}
(
definition

19
):

\mathtt{size}(\mathbf{G})=\mathtt{size}(\thesis\Gamma)+|V_{G}|+\sum_{e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}X}|X|.

The size of
\thesis\Gamma
(
definition

24
,
appendix

0.B
) is by

proposition

9
the sum of the number of atom occurrences
in
\Gamma
(notation
\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)
) with the number of logical symbols,
also called the
degree of
\Gamma
(notation
\mathtt{deg}(\Gamma)
). Because

\Gamma
is sharing-free by hypothesis, the number of atom occurrences coincides with
the number of names, i.e.
\mathtt{\#at}(\thesis\Gamma)=|\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)|
.

Observe also that the sum at the end of the expression is taken not over the set
of branches of
G
, but over all edge-branch pairs, i.e. a branch may be counted
more than once if it has multiple edges. Because
e\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}X
implies
e\subseteq X
,
i.e. no branch in a bl-graph is empty, the sum provides an upper bound to the
number of edge-branch pairs as well as to that of edges and branches, i.e. we have

|E_{G}|,|\mathtt{Br}(G)|\leq|{\mathrel{\Yleft}_{G}}|\leq\mathtt{size}(\mathbf{G}).

We have to check three conditions separately (
definition

17
):

1.

V_{G}=\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)
: checking name set equality is worst-case
polynomial in their cardinalities, and constructing the set
\mathtt{names}(\Gamma)

from
\Gamma
requires polynomial time in the size of
\thesis\Gamma
;

2.

\mathtt{Br}(G)=\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
: this is the most complex problem.
Generating just one element in
\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
amounts to persistently expanding
one branch of a
\mathtt{GS4}^{\mathcal{N}}
derivation of
\Gamma
until an atomic
sequent is reached; the length of such a branch is known to be bounded by the
complexity degree of
\thesis\Gamma

[
30
]
, hence the cost of generating
one branch name is polynomially bounded in the size of
\thesis\Gamma
. However,
the total number of branches is in the worst case exponential in the complexity
degree of
\thesis\Gamma
: thus we cannot take the naive approach of constructing
the whole set
\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
, then testing for equality. We describe an
informal algorithm: the idea is to generate the branch names of
\Gamma

incrementally, match them with some element from the set
\mathtt{Br}(G)
and
erase that element. For every matching attempt, either the algorithm fails or
the number of branches still to be matched decreases: in this way the number
of generated branch names is always bounded by the cardinality of
\mathtt{Br}(G)
.
Let
S
be the branch set to test (initially
S=\mathtt{Br}(G)
),
\Delta

the sequent to test against (initially
\Delta=\Gamma
); the algorithm has
three phases:

•

problem reduction phase:
if the sequent
\Delta
to test
against contains a disjunction, i.e. is of the form
\Delta^{\prime},A\lor B
,
then replace it with
\Delta^{\prime},A,B
. If it contains no disjunction but
at least a conjunction, i.e. is of the form
\Delta^{\prime},A\land B
, then
replace it with
\Delta^{\prime},A
and append
\Delta^{\prime},B
to a list of
sequents to test against later. By
proposition

3
,
the set of branches to test against has not changed;

•

matching phase:
if the sequent
\Delta
to test against is atomic,
then it has a unique branch
X=\mathtt{names}(\Delta)
. We search for that branch
in
S
: if not found, then
X\in\mathtt{Br}(\Gamma)
but
X\notin\mathtt{Br}(G)
,
and we stop; if found, we erase
X
from
S
and move on to the backtracking
phase;

•

backtracking phase:
if both
S
and the list of delayed sequents are
empty, then we’re done. If
S
is empty but the list is not, then some branches
are missing from
\mathtt{Br}(G)
and we stop. If
S
has some elements but
the list is empty, then there are excess branches in
\mathtt{Br}(G)
and we
stop. If both are non-empty, we pick the first element of the list as the new

\Delta
, erase it from the list and move back to the reduction phase.

It is clear that the number of steps in the reduction phase is bounded by the complexity
degree of the active sequent
\Delta
, which always decreases: when it reaches zero,
we move to the matching phase. The matching phase either fails or decreases the
size of the set
B
; once the set
B
becomes empty, the algorithm stops:
thus the size of
B
bounds the number of future reduction phases. Observe now that
a reduction step requires polynomial time in the size of the active sequent;
a matching step requires polynomial time in the cardinality of the generated branch
and the sum of the cardinalities of all elements of
B
. Backtracking steps require
constant time. Every measure mentioned above is itself bounded by
\mathtt{size}(\mathbf{G})
.
We have then a polynomial bound on the execution time of the algorithm with parameter

(\mathtt{size}(\mathbf{G}))^{3}
.

3.

for all
xy\in E_{G}
,
\Gamma[x]=\overline{\Gamma[y]}
: we observed at the
beginning of the proof that
\mathtt{size}(\mathbf{G})
bounds
|E_{G}|
; finding
the atom associated to a given name in
\Gamma
is polynomial in the size
of
\thesis\Gamma
. ∎

(a)

The initial derivation, with a unique cut-rule. Assume names
x,y,z,s,t,u,v,w\in\mathcal{N}
are pairwise distinct. There is an alternating path
connecting
{\overline{\alpha}}^{v}
with
{\alpha}^{w}
. Because the conclusion
is atomic, there is only one branch name up to names in the interface, hence all
edges are compatible.
